mainTopic: Doubtful claims to money: the robber's silence, רבי עקיבא on taking money away because of a doubt, a שומר's duty to keep track, and why the משנה gives both the money and vessels cases
overview: This amud finishes explaining two versions of how a robber reacts when several people each say 'you robbed me.' One version says he protests loudly, and the other says his silence proves nothing. רב ספרא then explains that 'he places the stolen item between them' means the money stays put until someone proves it is his. Next אביי asks רבא how רבי עקיבא can make the robber pay everyone because of a doubt, when in the case of the house that fell on a son and his mother רבי עקיבא leaves the property where it is. רבא answers that a sure claim against an unsure one is different from two unsure sides. Our משנה, where both sides are unsure yet the robber pays both, is explained as describing what he must do to clear himself before Heaven. רבינא then challenges רבא's rule that a שומר given two bundles must keep track, and רב אשי answers that the shepherd never knew the animals were put in his flock. Finally the גמרא explains why the משנה needs both the money case and the case of two vessels.

steps.title: Explaining the two versions: 'screams' versus 'silent'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind each version of the robber's reaction to the claimants.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The robber] screams. The one who says 'the other screams' holds that silence would count as admitting. The one who says 'the other is silent' holds that silence here is not an admission. The robber can say: 'I kept quiet to each one because I thought, maybe this is the one I robbed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why one version says the robber 'screams' and the other says he is 'silent.' The two versions disagree about whether staying quiet counts as admitting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'screams' version holds that silence counts as a הודאה, so it had to describe him protesting loudly. The 'silent' version holds that here, silence proves nothing. He kept quiet to each person only because each one might be the real victim, not because he owes all of them.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the 'silent' version holds that silence is never an admission. It only says that in this case, with several people claiming, his silence has a different explanation.

phrases.english: screams.
phrases.notes: This word finishes the line from before: one version says the robber screams at each claimant that he doesn't know them.

phrases.english: The one who says 'the other screams'
[holds that] silence is like admission.
And the one who says 'the other is silent'
[holds that] silence here is not like admission,
since he can say to him:
The fact that I was silent to each and every one
is because I said: perhaps this is he.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes explaining the two versions of the ברייתא quoted just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'screams' version holds silence would be an admission. The 'silent' version holds silence here is not an admission, because each claimant might be the real victim.
steps.whatToRemember: The two versions differ on one point: does the robber's silence toward each claimant count as admitting he owes each one?

steps.title: Quoting the ruling: he places the stolen item between them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from the ברייתא so it can examine it next.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: He places the stolen item between them and leaves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ruling from the ברייתא: the robber puts the stolen item down among the claimants and walks away. This is a setup line, preparing for a challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain meaning is that the robber has done his part once he puts the money in front of all the claimants. The next step will ask whether that is really allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: he places the stolen item between them

phrases.english: The Master said:
He places the stolen item between them
and withdraws.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: מַנִּיחַ גְּזֵילָה בֵּינֵיהֶם וּמִסְתַּלֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to a different line of the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The robber puts the stolen item before the claimants and steps away.

steps.title: Challenge: can they all just grab it? רב's rule about doubtful placement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that letting everyone take the money goes against רב's rule. Under that rule, an item that might belong to someone is not handed over without proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do they all take it and leave? But רבי אבא בר זבדא said in רב's name: whenever it is unclear whether an item was put down on purpose, a person should not pick it up in the first place, and if he did, he should not give it back [without proof].
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling from step 2. If the robber walks away, the claimants will grab the money, and the real owner may lose it. רב teaches that in a doubtful case we do not hand an item over without proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's rule is about a found item that may have been placed down on purpose by its owner. Since the owner may come back, one should not move it. If someone already took it, he should not give it to just anyone who claims it. So here too, the robber should not let the money go to people who have no proof.

keyTerms.meaning: a doubt whether the item was put down on purpose
at the outset, before the fact

phrases.english: And they all take it and go?
But didn't Rabbi Abba bar Zavda say
that Rav said:
In any case of doubtful placement,
phrases.notes: An item that its owner may have put down on purpose, so it isn't really 'lost.'

phrases.english: at the outset he should not take it,
and if he took it, he should not return it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשָׁקְלִי לַהּ כּוּלְּהוּ וְאָזְלִי? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling quoted in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the robber places the item between the claimants and leaves.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב's rule shows that in a doubtful case we don't let unproven claimants take an item. Leaving the money for all of them to grab goes against that.

steps.title: רב ספרא: he just leaves it there
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא reads the ברייתא as saying the money stays put until the real owner is clear, not that the claimants grab it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: [The ruling means] 'and he should leave it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא answers the challenge. 'Places it' means the money is left where it is, not handed out to the claimants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'places' is now read as 'leaves it be' until one claimant proves it is his. That fits רב's rule, because nobody takes the money without proof.

keyTerms.meaning: and he should leave it (in place)

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
And he should leave it.
phrases.notes: He means the money stays put (with the robber or in בית דין) until someone proves it's his.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Places it between them' meant the claimants may take it.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means the robber leaves the money in place until the owner is proven.
steps.whatToRemember: 'מניח' here means leaving the money in place until proof comes, not letting everyone grab it.

steps.title: אביי's inference: רבי עקיבא takes money away because of a doubt
steps.stepSummary: From רבי עקיבא's ruling that the robber must pay each claimant, אביי concludes that רבי עקיבא takes money away even when there is only a doubt.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: Didn't רבי עקיבא say that this is not the way to free him from his sin until he pays the stolen amount to each and every one? So it seems that because of a doubt we take money away, and we do not say 'leave the money with its owner.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי draws a principle out of רבי עקיבא's ruling about someone who robbed one of five people. This sets up a contradiction in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The robber only truly owes one person, but רבי עקיבא makes him pay all of them. That means taking money from him even though, for each claimant, it is only a doubt that he owes them. This goes against the usual rule, 'אוקים ממונא בחזקת מריה'.

keyTerms.meaning: we take money away because of a doubt
leave the money with its presumed owner

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rava:
Didn't Rabbi Akiva say
'This is not the way
that frees him from sin

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיְּשַׁלֵּם גְּזֵילָה לְכֹל חַד וְחַד?
phrases.english: until he pays the stolen item to each and every one'?
phrases.notes: This is רבי עקיבא's ruling about someone who robbed one of five people and doesn't know which one.

phrases.english: Apparently, because of a doubt we take money away,
and we don't say
'Leave the money in the possession of its owner.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרָבָא: מִי אָמַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about רבי עקיבא's opinion in the same case of robbing one of five.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי עקיבא holds we take money away because of a doubt.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי עקיבא's ruling that the robber must pay each of the five claimants.

steps.title: Contradiction: the house that fell on a son and his mother
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה where רבי עקיבא rules that property stays where it is when there is a doubt. That seems to contradict step 5.
steps.simpleTranslation: They pointed out a contradiction: A house fell on a man and his mother. The son's heirs say the mother died first; the mother's heirs say the son died first. Both groups of תנאים agree they split it. And רבי עקיבא said: 'I agree here that the property stays in its presumed ownership!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows a case where רבי עקיבא does not take money away because of a doubt. That goes against what אביי just inferred.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is unclear who died first, so it is unclear who inherits. Here רבי עקיבא says the property stays where it is, which is exactly 'אוקים ממונא בחזקת מריה'. So how can he force the robber to pay everyone because of a doubt?

keyTerms.meaning: and they pointed out a contradiction
property stays in its presumed ownership

phrases.english: And they pointed out a contradiction:
A house fell on him and on his mother,
the son's heirs say:
The mother died first.
And the mother's heirs say:
The son died first.
These and those agree that they split it.
phrases.notes: 'These and those' are בית שמאי and בית הלל, who argue in similar cases but agree here.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Akiva said:
I agree in this case
that the property stays in its presumed ownership!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּרְמִינְהִי: נָפַל הַבַּיִת עָלָיו וְעַל אִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the principle אביי drew in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that רבי עקיבא takes money away because of a doubt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the collapsed-house case, רבי עקיבא leaves the property where it is despite the doubt. That is the opposite of taking money away because of a doubt.
steps.whyThisMatters: It forces the גמרא to explain why רבי עקיבא treats the robber differently from an ordinary doubt about who owns money.

steps.title: רבא distinguishes the two cases: both unsure versus one side sure
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the collapsed house case is שמא ושמא, while the robbed-from-five case is ברי ושמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, both sides are unsure. When someone robbed one of five people, one side is sure and the other is unsure.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the contradiction from step 6 by showing that the two cases are built differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the collapsed house case, nobody knows what happened, so both claims are just guesses and the property stays where it is. In the robbery case, each victim says 'I am sure it was me' while the robber only says 'I don't know.' A sure claim against an unsure one is strong enough for רבי עקיבא to take money away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Certain' against 'maybe': one side is sure and the other is unsure

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying רבי עקיבא always takes money away when there is a doubt. He only does so when a sure claim faces an unsure one.

phrases.english: He said to him: There, it is 'maybe' against 'maybe';
phrases.notes: 'There' means the collapsed house case brought in step 6, where nobody knows who died first.

phrases.english: but one who robbed one of five is 'certain' against 'maybe.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (אוקימתא by type of claim)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי עקיבא seemed to contradict himself, taking money away in one doubt case and leaving property in place in another.
steps.terutzMaskana: When both sides are unsure, property stays in place. When the claimants are sure and the defendant is unsure, רבי עקיבא takes money away.

steps.title: Challenge from our משנה, where both sides are unsure yet he pays both
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה is a case where both sides are unsure, yet the robber pays each person a מנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But our משנה here: he said to two people, 'I robbed one of you of a מנה.' That is a case of 'maybe' against 'maybe,' and it teaches that he gives a מנה to this one and a מנה to that one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא's distinction using the משנה on our daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה, the robber does not know whom he robbed, and the two people do not know either. That is שמא ושמא, just like the collapsed house. Yet the robber must pay both of them, so money is taken away even when both sides are unsure, which breaks רבא's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred דינרים

phrases.english: But our משנה here:
he said to two people:
'I robbed one of you of a מנה,'
which is 'maybe' against 'maybe,'

phrases.aramaic: וְקָתָנֵי: נוֹתֵן לָזֶה מָנֶה וְלָזֶה מָנֶה.
phrases.english: and it teaches: he gives this one a מנה and that one a מנה.

steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that רבי עקיבא does not take money away when both sides are unsure.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Our משנה (assumed to follow רבי עקיבא) is שמא ושמא, yet it makes the robber pay both people.

steps.title: How do we know our משנה follows רבי עקיבא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that our משנה follows רבי עקיבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that it follows רבי עקיבא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to check a hidden assumption in the challenge. This sets up the proof in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge only works if our משנה follows רבי עקיבא, because רבא's rule is about רבי עקיבא's view. If the משנה followed someone else, there would be no problem.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do we know?

phrases.english: And from where do we know that it follows רבי עקיבא?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Checks an assumption behind the challenge in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that our משנה follows רבי עקיבא.

steps.title: רבי טרפון concedes, and he concedes to רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says רבי טרפון agrees in this case, and the one he usually argues with, and so agrees with here, is רבי עקיבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it teaches about that משנה: רבי טרפון agrees in the case where someone says to two people, 'I robbed one of you of a מנה and I don't know which of you, etc.' To whom does he agree? Is it not to רבי עקיבא, his usual opponent?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves that our משנה follows רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'agrees' implies that רבי טרפון is giving in to someone else's view. Since רבי טרפון usually argues with רבי עקיבא, he must be agreeing with רבי עקיבא here. So paying both people is רבי עקיבא's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Agrees (concedes to the other side's view)

phrases.english: Because it teaches about that one:
רבי טרפון agrees in a case where one says to two people,
'I robbed one of you of a מנה
and I don't know which of you, etc.'
phrases.notes: כו׳ means 'etc.': the rest of the line, that he pays each one, is assumed.

phrases.english: To whom does he agree?
Is it not to רבי עקיבא, his opponent?

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא says רבי טרפון agrees, and the one he agrees with must be his usual opponent, רבי עקיבא.

steps.title: How do we know both sides in our משנה are unsure?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that our משנה is a case of שמא ושמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that it is 'maybe' against 'maybe'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks the second assumption behind the challenge. This sets up the proofs in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the two people in the משנה were each sure, it would be ברי ושמא, and רבא's rule would explain why the robber pays. So the challenge needs both sides to be unsure.

phrases.english: And from where do we know that it is 'maybe' against 'maybe'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Checks a second assumption behind the challenge in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Proof that in our משנה the two people are unsure, not sure.

steps.title: Two proofs that both sides are unsure
steps.stepSummary: The משנה never says they demand payment, and רבי חייא teaches that each one says 'I don't know.'
steps.simpleTranslation: First, it does not teach that they are demanding payment from him. And besides, רבי חייא taught: this one says 'I don't know' and that one says 'I don't know.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two proofs that the people in our משנה are unsure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the two people were sure, the משנה would describe them suing the robber, but it does not. On top of that, רבי חייא's ברייתא says outright that each one says 'I don't know.' So the challenge in step 8 stands.

phrases.english: First, it does not teach 'they are demanding from him.'
And besides, didn't רבי חייא teach:
this one says 'I don't know'
and that one says 'I don't know.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 11, which strengthens the challenge of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה does not mention them demanding payment, and רבי חייא says each one says 'I don't know.'

steps.title: The משנה is about a robber clearing himself before Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The משנה describes a robber who wants to clear himself before Heaven, not a payment a court forces.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we already explained it as a case where he comes to fulfill his duty to Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 8 using an explanation of the משנה given earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying both people is only what the robber must do to fully repent before Heaven. A court would not force him to pay when both sides are unsure. So רבא's rule holds: when both sides are unsure, the court does not take money away, even according to רבי עקיבא.

keyTerms.meaning: We explained it (set it in a specific case)
To fulfill one's duty to Heaven, beyond what a court requires

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, רבי עקיבא takes money away only in a case of בָּרִי וְשֶׁמָּא. When both sides are unsure, property stays in place. The משנה's 'pay both' is only the extra step a robber takes to clear himself before Heaven.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'pay both' as a court ruling. It describes what the robber should do to be right with Heaven, not what a court makes him pay.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets apart what a court can force from what a person must do to fully repent, a split that comes up often in the laws of money.

phrases.english: But we already explained it
phrases.notes: This points back to earlier on our daf, where the גמרא explained the משנה this same way.

phrases.english: as a case where he comes to fulfill his duty to Heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא אוֹקֵימְנָא לַהּ בְּבָא לָצֵאת יְדֵי שָׁמַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 8 after steps 9-12 confirmed it was strong.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (the ruling is only about a duty to Heaven)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to make a court take money away even when both sides are unsure, according to רבי עקיבא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a robber who wants to clear himself before Heaven. A court does not take money away when both sides are unsure.

steps.title: רבינא challenges רבא's rule about two bundles
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי whether רבא really said that a שומר given two separate bundles must pay attention. Another ruling, from רבא or רב פפא, says a shepherd may simply leave the animals between the two owners.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: Did רבא really say that whenever deposits come in two separate bundles, the bailee should have paid attention? But didn't רבא (or some say רב פפא) say that everyone agrees that when two people deposit with a shepherd, the shepherd puts the animals between them and walks away?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא brings a ruling that seems to contradict רבא's rule that a שומר must keep track of who gave him what.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shepherd also receives two separate deposits, from two different owners. If he had to keep track, he could not just leave the animals and walk away. So the shepherd ruling seems to say that a שומר does not have to pay attention.

keyTerms.meaning: bundles; separate packages of a deposit
he should have paid careful attention
walks away; removes himself from the case
and some say (a second opinion about who said it)

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
And did Rava really say
that whenever it is in two separate bundles
he should have paid careful attention?
phrases.notes: He should have noticed which bundle came from which person, so he can't just say 'I don't know.'

phrases.english: But didn't Rava say,
and some say it was Rav Pappa:
Everyone agrees about two people
who deposited animals with a shepherd,
that the shepherd places the animals between them and walks away!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the שמא ושמא discussion and challenges רבא's earlier rule about two bundles.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's rule that a שומר with two separate bundles should have paid attention
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The shepherd also held two separate deposits, yet he may walk away without paying. That suggests a שומר does not have to keep track.

steps.title: The shepherd never agreed to watch those animals
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the shepherd case is about animals put into his flock without his knowledge.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, it is when they put the animals into the shepherd's flock without his knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי shows that the shepherd case is different, so it does not contradict רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שומר who knowingly accepts two deposits should keep track of them. The shepherd never knew the animals were given to him, so nobody expected him to notice whose they were. רבא's rule still stands.
steps.whatToRemember: A שומר has to keep track only of deposits he knowingly accepted. If animals were slipped into a shepherd's flock without his knowledge, he can leave them between the owners and walk away.

phrases.english: He said to him:
There, it is when they deposited
into the shepherd's flock
without his knowledge.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם כְּשֶׁהִפְקִידוּ בְּעֶדְרוֹ שֶׁל רוֹעֶה שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by showing the shepherd case is a different situation.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the shepherd case is about a deposit made without his knowledge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The shepherd ruling seemed to show that any שומר of two deposits does not have to keep track.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a שומר who knowingly accepted the deposits must keep track. The shepherd did not know, so he is exempt.

steps.title: The משנה's case of two vessels, and the claim that both cases are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה, two vessels of very different value. It says the משנה needed to teach both this case and the money case.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: And likewise, two vessels, one worth a maneh and one worth a thousand zuz, etc. And both cases are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the vessels case and claims that teaching it alongside the money case is not extra. This line sets up the next step, which explains why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The vessels case seems to say nothing new beyond the money case. The word צריכא, 'it is necessary', tells us each case teaches something the other does not. The explanation follows in the next two steps.

keyTerms.meaning: a maneh, a coin worth one hundred זוז
a zuz, a common silver coin
and it is necessary (both cases are needed)

phrases.english: And likewise, two vessels:
one worth a maneh
and one worth a thousand zuz, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' means the rest of the משנה: each person claims the expensive vessel is his.

phrases.english: And it is necessary.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן שְׁנֵי כֵלִים אֶחָד יָפֶה מָנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The vessels case is not repeating the money case. Both cases are needed.

steps.title: Why the vessels case is needed
steps.stepSummary: From the money case alone, we might think the רבנן split things only because nobody loses anything. With vessels, where the big vessel is lost, we might think they agree with רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if the משנה had taught only the first case, we would say the רבנן rule that way there because there is no loss. But here, where the big vessel is lost, we might say they agree with רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the vessels case adds that the money case could not teach.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With money, the רבנן give each person a maneh and put the rest aside, and nothing is damaged. With vessels, paying the second person means selling or losing the big vessel. That loss might make the רבנן agree with רבי יוסי to put everything aside, so the משנה teaches that they do not.

phrases.english: For if it had taught us only that first case:
phrases.notes: The first case is the money case, where one person deposited a maneh and the other deposited two hundred.

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does the משנה need to add the vessels case?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Without it, we might think the רבנן agree with רבי יוסי when splitting would cause a loss.

steps.title: Why the money case is needed, so both are necessary
steps.stepSummary: From the vessels case alone, we might think רבי יוסי rules his way only because of the loss, and agrees with the רבנן about money. So both cases are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the argument had been stated only in the vessels case, we would say that רבי יוסי rules his way there. But in the money case, we might say he agrees with the רבנן. So both are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the צריכא: the money case teaches something about רבי יוסי that the vessels case could not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From the vessels case alone, we might think רבי יוסי puts everything aside only to avoid losing the big vessel. The money case shows that he holds his view even when nothing is lost. So each case teaches something about a different side of the argument.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה needs both cases. The vessels case shows the רבנן split even when a vessel is lost. The money case shows רבי יוסי puts everything aside even when nothing is lost.
steps.confusionAlert: Each case teaches about a different side. The vessels case is needed for the רבנן's view, and the money case is needed for רבי יוסי's view.

steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both cases are needed. The רבנן split even when there is a loss, and רבי יוסי puts everything aside even when there is no loss.
